lessonActivities.title: Already: Done Sooner Than Expected! ⏰
lessonActivities.content:
Already is used to say that something has happened earlier than expected or earlier than it might have happened. ⏰

Core Structure:

ComponentPositionExample
have/hasFirstI have
alreadyMiddlealready
past participleLastfinished

Typical Exchanges:

Speaker ASpeaker BMeaning
"Hurry up Susan. Breakfast is ready!""I have already had breakfast thanks. I woke up early."Action completed before expected time
"Here is a book you might like.""I have already read it — I found it interesting too."Action completed before the offer

Pattern: have/has + already + past participle

Fun fact: "Already" can also express surprise: "Have you finished already?!" 🎉
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Quick Rule: Already goes between have/has and the past participle: have already finished.

lessonActivities.title: Still: Things That Keep Going 🔄
lessonActivities.content:
Still is used to refer to continuing situations. Something that started in the past and continues now. 🔄

Position Rules:

Verb TypePositionExample
Verb beAfter beI am still waiting.
Main verbBefore main verbShe still works there.

Examples in Context:

SentenceDurationImplied Meaning
They have been married for 40 years and they still love each other.40 yearsContinues despite long time
I moved to this town five years ago and I am still living here.5 yearsContinues from past to present
Are you still smoking? I thought you had stopped!OngoingSurprise at continuation
It started raining early this morning and it is still raining!Since morningEmphasis on duration

Fun fact: "Still" often expresses surprise that a situation continues! 😲
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Memory trick: Still goes before the main verb or after be: am still, still works.

lessonActivities.title: Always: Every Time, All the Time 💫
lessonActivities.content:
Always is used to refer to something that happens regularly, very frequently, or forever. 💫

Standard Usage — Habits & Routines:

PatternExampleMeaning
Subject + always + verbI always send cards at Christmas.Regular habit
Subject + always + verbSue always takes the 8 o'clock train to work.Fixed routine
Subject + will + always + verbI promise I will always love you.Forever commitment

Special Usage — Complaint Form:

StructureExampleEmotion
Subject + be + always + verb-ingAlex is always complaining about his job.Irritation
Subject + be + always + verb-ingShe is always losing her keys!Frustration

The Secret: always + present continuous expresses irritation about a repeated, annoying habit.

Fun fact: Using always with present continuous is a classic way to complain in English! 😤
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Pro tip: For complaints, use present continuous + always: "He is always losing his keys!"

lessonActivities.title: Yet: Waiting for Something to Happen ⏳
lessonActivities.content:
Yet is used in questions, to ask if something expected has happened, and in negative sentences. ⏳

Key Rule: Yet always goes at the END of the sentence or clause!

UseStructureExample
QuestionsHave/Has + subject + past participle + yet?Has the postman arrived yet?
QuestionsHave/Has + subject + past participle + yet?Have you booked your ticket yet?
NegativeSubject + have/has + not + past participle + yetThe book I ordered has not arrived yet.
NegativeSubject + have/has + not + yet + past participleJulie has not yet decided whether she is going to join us.

Meaning Notes:

SentenceMeaning
The book has not arrived yet.I am still waiting.
They have not set the date of their wedding yet.Still undecided, expected soon.

Fun fact: "Yet" always goes at the END of the sentence or clause! 🎯
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Never forget: Yet goes at the END of the sentence. Use it with present perfect.

lessonActivities.title: Yet: Meaning Nevertheless ⚡
lessonActivities.content:
Yet can also be used to link two clauses or contrasting ideas (like "nevertheless" or "nonetheless"). ⚡

Contrast Usage:

PatternExampleMeaning
Clause 1 + comma + yet + clause 2Olivia was offered an interesting job with good pay, yet she refused it.Unexpected contrast
Clause 1 + comma + yet + clause 2Charlie felt alone in the world, yet he was surrounded by friends.Surprising contradiction
Adjective + yet + adjectiveMr. Harding was a strict yet fair teacher.Balanced qualities

Emphasis Usage:

StructureExampleMeaning
yet another + nounSunday will be yet another rainy day.One more in a series
yet againThe photocopier is out of order yet again!Repeating frustration

Fun fact: This use of yet comes from Old English and is very common in literature! 📚
examples: He felt alone, yet he was surrounded by friends.
She sings beautifully, yet she prefers to accompany others.
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Rule: When yet means "but," it usually has a comma before it.

lessonActivities.title: Already, Still, Always & Yet Together 🎯
lessonActivities.content:
Let us compare all four adverbs side by side! 🎯

AdverbMeaningExampleTense Used
AlreadyCompleted earlyI have already eaten.Present perfect
StillContinuingI am still hungry.Present continuous / simple
AlwaysRegular / habitI always eat at 7.Present simple
YetNot finishedI have not eaten yet.Present perfect negative/question

Tense Patterns Summary:

AdverbTense PatternExample
AlreadyPresent perfectShe has already left.
StillPresent continuous / present simpleHe is still working. / He still works.
AlwaysPresent simple (complaints: present continuous)They always arrive late. / He is always complaining.
YetPresent perfect negative/questionHave you finished yet? / I have not finished yet.

Fun fact: Many languages do not have exact equivalents for these four words, making them tricky for learners! 🌍
examples: Have you already left? No, I am still here.
I always wait for you, yet you are never on time.
functions: Choosing the correct adverb for context
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Decision tree: Finished? → already. Continuing? → still. Regular? → always. Not finished? → yet.

lessonActivities.title: Avoid These Common Errors ❌
lessonActivities.content:
Let us master the most common errors with these adverbs! ❌

Common Mistakes Table:

Wrong ❌Why It's WrongRight ✅
I have finished yet.Yet is for negative/questions, not positive completionI have already finished.
I yet have not seen it.Wrong word order — yet must be at the endI have not seen it yet.
She is always late? (question intonation only)Missing question inversionIs she always late?
I still am working.Wrong position — still goes after beI am still working.
She is yet here.Wrong adverb — yet means not finishedShe is still here.

Position Rules Summary:

AdverbPositionExample
AlreadyBetween have/has and past participleI have already finished.
StillBefore main verb or after beI am still waiting. / She still works.
YetAt the end of the clauseI have not seen it yet.
AlwaysAfter be, before other verbsShe is always late. / She always arrives late.

Fun fact: Native speakers sometimes break these rules in casual speech, but exams expect formal correctness! 🎓
examples: ❌ She is yet here → ✅ She is still here.
❌ I yet have not seen it → ✅ I have not seen it yet.
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Remember: Already = positive. Yet = negative/question. Still = positive/negative continuation.

lessonActivities.title: Master Level: Nuanced Meanings 🏆
lessonActivities.content:
You have come so far! Let us tackle the advanced nuances. 🌟

Special Case 1: Formal "have yet to"

StructureExampleEquivalent Meaning
Subject + have/has + yet to + base verbWe have yet to find out the cause.We still have not found out.
Subject + have/has + yet to + base verbI have yet to understand the problem.I still do not understand.

Special Case 2: American English Variation

VarietyExampleNotes
British EnglishI have already eaten.Present perfect standard
American EnglishI already ate.Past simple also acceptable

Special Case 3: Advanced "better yet"

StructureExampleMeaning
or better yetDo not overcook the fish, or better yet, eat it raw.An even better suggestion

Mastery Checklist:

SkillStatus
Already for early completion✅
Still for continuation✅
Always for habits and complaints✅
Yet for unfinished actions✅
Yet for contrast✅
"Have yet to" formal structure✅

Fun fact: "Have yet to" is considered very elegant and is common in academic writing! 🎓
examples: I have yet to understand the problem.
The photocopier is out of order yet again!
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Master level: "Have yet to" is formal and elegant. Use it in academic or professional writing.

writingActivities.question: Write about things you have already done today using already + present perfect. Include at least 2 sentences with already.
writingActivities.hint: Use have/has + already + past participle. Example: I have already eaten breakfast and I have already read the news.

writingActivities.question: Describe things that are still happening in your life. Use still + present continuous or present simple in at least 2 sentences.
writingActivities.hint: Use still to show continuation. Example: I am still learning English. I still live in the same house.

writingActivities.question: Write about your plans and unfinished tasks using yet in negative sentences and questions. Include at least 1 question and 1 negative sentence.
writingActivities.hint: Use Have you...yet? for questions and haven't/hasn't...yet for negatives. Example: I haven't finished my homework yet. Have you called her yet?

writingActivities.question: Write about your habits using always + present simple. Describe 3 things you always do.
writingActivities.hint: Use always with present simple for habits. Example: I always drink coffee in the morning. She always takes the bus.

writingActivities.question: Describe changes in your town or city using already and still. Show what has changed and what has stayed the same.
writingActivities.hint: Use already for completed changes and still for things that haven't changed. Example: They have already built a new hospital, but the old school is still there.

writingActivities.question: Write two contrasting sentences using yet to mean nevertheless. Connect two unexpected ideas.
writingActivities.hint: Use yet like 'but' or 'nevertheless'. Example: She was very tired, yet she finished the marathon.

gameActivities.question: Choose the correct word:
gameActivities.hint: This is a positive sentence about something completed. Use already for completed actions.

gameActivities.question: Which sentence is correct?
gameActivities.sentence: She ____ lives in the same house.
gameActivities.hint: This sentence talks about a continuing situation. Use still for things that continue.

gameActivities.question: Advanced: Complete with the most precise word:
gameActivities.sentence: The offer was generous, ____ she refused it.
gameActivities.hint: The two parts of the sentence contrast with each other. Use yet to mean 'nevertheless'.

quizActivities.question: What does already express?
quizActivities.hint: Already is used when something happens sooner than expected.
quizActivities.explanation: Already indicates that an action is complete, often sooner than expected.

quizActivities.question: Which sentence uses still correctly?
options: I am still waiting for you
I still am waiting for you
I waiting still am for you
I am waiting for you still
quizActivities.correctAnswer: I am still waiting for you
quizActivities.hint: Still goes before the main verb or after the verb 'be'.
quizActivities.explanation: After 'be': am still waiting. Before other verbs: still works.

quizActivities.question: Where does yet usually go in a sentence?
quizActivities.hint: Yet typically appears at the end of questions and negative sentences.
quizActivities.explanation: Yet goes at the end: Have you finished yet? I haven't finished yet.

quizActivities.question: Choose the correct form:
quizActivities.hint: Questions expecting a completion use yet at the end.
quizActivities.explanation: Yet is used in questions to ask if something expected has happened.

quizActivities.question: Which shows a habit?
quizActivities.sentence: Choose the sentence that describes a regular action.
options: I always brush my teeth before bed
I am still brushing my teeth
I have already brushed my teeth
I haven't brushed my teeth yet
quizActivities.correctAnswer: I always brush my teeth before bed
quizActivities.hint: Always with present simple describes habits and routines.
quizActivities.explanation: Always + present simple expresses regular habits.

quizActivities.question: What is the correct negative with yet?
quizActivities.hint: Use present perfect negative + yet at the end.
quizActivities.explanation: The standard form is haven't/hasn't + past participle + yet. Yet goes at the end.

quizActivities.question: Advanced: 'He is always losing his keys!' This expresses:
quizActivities.hint: Always + present continuous often shows the speaker is annoyed.
quizActivities.explanation: Present continuous + always expresses annoyance about repeated actions.

quizActivities.question: Choose the best sentence:
quizActivities.sentence: They have been married 50 years and they ____ love each other.
quizActivities.hint: This describes a continuing situation over 50 years.
quizActivities.explanation: Still shows that a situation continues over a long period.

quizActivities.question: Which uses yet as contrast?
quizActivities.sentence: Choose the sentence with contrastive yet.
options: She was tired, yet she kept working
quizActivities.correctAnswer: She was tired, yet she kept working
quizActivities.hint: Contrastive yet means 'nevertheless' and links two contrasting ideas.
quizActivities.explanation: Yet can mean 'nevertheless' when linking two contrasting clauses.

quizActivities.question: What tense usually goes with already?
quizActivities.hint: Already connects past actions to the present.
quizActivities.explanation: Already is typically used with present perfect: have/has + already + past participle.

quizActivities.question: Which is correct?
quizActivities.hint: Have yet to + infinitive is a formal structure meaning 'still have not'.
quizActivities.explanation: Have yet to + verb is a formal equivalent of still haven't + past participle.

quizActivities.question: Identify the error:
quizActivities.sentence: I have finished my dinner yet.
quizActivities.hint: Positive completed actions use already, not yet.
quizActivities.explanation: Yet is for negatives and questions. Already is for positive completed actions.

quizActivities.question: Which question is correct?
quizActivities.hint: Yet goes at the end of the question.
quizActivities.explanation: In questions, yet always occupies the end position: subject + verb + yet?

quizActivities.question: Complete the sentence:
quizActivities.sentence: I promise I will ____ love you.
quizActivities.explanation: Always expresses something that will happen regularly or forever.

quizActivities.question: Complete the sentence:
quizActivities.sentence: The book I ordered hasn't arrived ____.
quizActivities.hint: Negative present perfect + expectation uses yet at the end.
quizActivities.explanation: In negative present perfect sentences, yet goes at the end to show expectation.

spellingActivities.hint: Used to say something happened earlier than expected
spellingActivities.sentence: I have already finished my homework.

spellingActivities.hint: Used for things that happen regularly or forever
spellingActivities.sentence: I always take the 8 o'clock train.

spellingActivities.hint: Without interruption - related to still and continuing actions
spellingActivities.sentence: It has been raining continuously for three hours.
